Introduction
Behaviour can be defined as an expressed course of action produced in organisms in response to stimulus from a
given situation.

It could simply be considered as what the animal does. The fundamental explanation of behavioural activity must
begin with a stimulus and end with a response.

Stimulus: Any change in the biotic and abiotic environments capable of eliciting or causing some sort of reaction
or response in a living organism. For example, temperature, pressure, radiation, gravity, or activities of other
organisms within the immediate environment.

Approaches to behavioural studies

   i.      Vitalistic approach
           Behavioural activities are explained in terms of what animals are seen to do in relation to changes in the
           environment. It involves total rejection of any study of the animal outside its natural environment. The
           technique is non-scientific since all the observations relate to past events which cannot be tested
           experimentally.
   ii.     Mechanistic approach
           It is an experimental approach and involves the study of particular aspects of behaviour under controlled
           conditions in a laboratory. It was pioneered by Pavlov and used extensively in psychological study. It
           may be criticized on the basis of the artificiality of the experimental conditions and the way in which
           results are interpreted.
   iii.    Ethological approach
           Ethology is the scientific study of animal behaviour. It explains responses observed in the field in terms
           of stimuli eliciting the behaviour. This was pioneered by Lorenz, von Frisch and Tinbergen. Ethologists
           have so far tried to answer questions about animal behaviour from four major areas:
               1. The evolutionary history:
               -How did various forms of behaviour evolved? i.e. (Innate/instinctive/genetic or
                   learned?)
               -How does the behaviour compare with similar behaviour in related species?
               2. Development:

Investigate how seasonal changes, food availability, and environmental cues serve as
proximate causes for migration in different species.

Migration in animals is often driven by proximate causes—those immediate environmental and
physiological triggers that lead individuals to move—distinct from ultimate causes, which
explain the evolutionary “why.” Three key proximate factors are seasonal changes, food
availability, and environmental cues. Below is an investigation of how each operates across
different taxa.

1. Seasonal Changes

Seasonal variation in photoperiod (day length), temperature, and precipitation acts as a reliable
calendar for many species:

   •   Photoperiodicity
          o Many birds (e.g., white‐crowned sparrows) sense increasing day length in late
             winter via light receptors in the brain. This stimulates the hypothalamus–
             pituitary–gonadal axis, raising levels of migratory restlessness (zugunruhe) and
             fat deposition before departure.
   •   Temperature shifts
          o Insects such as the painted lady butterfly overwinter in warmer zones; a drop in
             ambient temperature signals them to start breeding and subsequent northward
             movement in spring.
   •   Rainfall patterns
          o African ungulates (like wildebeest) initiate long treks in response to the onset of
             seasonal rains that trigger fresh grass growth.

Example: Arctic terns time their epic pole‐to‐pole migrations by increasingly lengthening days
as they head north in spring, then shortening days in autumn to signal the return south.

2. Food Availability

The rise and fall of resources, both in quantity and quality, often precipitate migratory
departures:

   •   Phenological tracking
          o Temperate hummingbirds synchronize migration with blooming phenology of
             nectar plants. When flowering peaks, they move into breeding ranges; as blooms
             fade, they depart.
   •   Resource depletion
          o Caribou in the Arctic follow green‐up of tundra vegetation each spring. When
             forage quality declines post‐summer, they migrate toward calving grounds rich in
             fresh, nutrient‐dense plants.

Beyond broad seasonal signals, more immediate weather and navigational cues fine‐tune

   •   Social cues
          o Flocking species may initiate collective departure when a critical proportion of
              individuals display migratory restlessness, reinforcing group cohesion and timing.

Example: European starlings listen for barometric pressure drops preceding storm systems; a
sharp fall in pressure can precipitate emergency movements to avoid adverse weather.

Physiological Mechanisms Underlying Proximate Triggers

   •   Hormonal regulation: Changes in day length alter melatonin secretion patterns,
       cascading into changes in thyroid hormones and gonadotropins, which together drive
       fattening and restlessness.
   •   Neurobiological integration: Light input via deep brain photoreceptors informs
       circadian and circannual clocks, ensuring migration aligns with optimal conditions.

Synthesis

While ultimate explanations for migration center on fitness benefits (e.g., breeding in safe zones,
exploiting rich feeding grounds), proximate causes—seasonal rhythms, resource fluctuations,
and sensory cues—provide the “how” by which animals time and orient their movements. By
decoding these immediate triggers, researchers can better predict shifts in migratory behavior
under climate change, habitat alteration, and other anthropogenic pressures.

When a species' primary food source becomes scarce or unavailable, adaptations in foraging
behavior may occur to ensure survival. These adaptations can manifest through behavioral,
physiological, and ecological changes that enable the species to find alternative resources,
optimize energy expenditure, and reduce competition. Here are some possible adaptations:

1. Broadening Diet Preferences (Dietary Generalization)

Species may adapt by becoming less specialized in their diet and consuming a wider variety of
food items. This dietary generalization allows them to exploit previously overlooked or less
preferred food sources. For example, a carnivore might include more plant-based foods in its
diet, or an insect that primarily feeds on one type of plant might shift to feeding on related
species.

2. Shifting Foraging Locations

Individuals may expand their range or move to new habitats in search of food. This might
include exploring areas where the food source is less depleted or venturing into habitats
previously avoided due to competition, predation, or environmental factors. Migration to more
resource-rich areas is a common strategy in highly mobile species.

3. Changing Foraging Times

Temporal shifts in foraging behavior can occur to avoid competition or predation. For example, a
species might become nocturnal or diurnal if their typical food source availability is higher at
those times. This change reduces reliance on a depleted food source by allowing access to other
resources that are available at specific times.

4. Development of New Foraging Techniques

Species may innovate or refine foraging techniques to access alternative resources. This can
include:

   •   Using tools to extract hard-to-reach or protected food sources.
   •   Altering hunting strategies to target new prey.
   •   Learning from other species or individuals about new food sources or techniques.

5. Increased Mobility and Exploration

Species might increase their range of movement, becoming more nomadic or exploratory to
locate dispersed or patchy resources. For example, animals might develop enhanced navigation
skills or invest more time in searching behavior to locate food in an unpredictable environment.

6. Changes in Social Behavior

For social species, changes might include:

   •   Forming smaller groups to reduce competition for limited resources.
   •   Sharing information about food sources more effectively within groups.
   •   Increased aggression or territorial behavior to secure access to scarce food.

7. Physiological Adjustments

Physiological adaptations might include:

   •   Slowing metabolic rates to conserve energy during food shortages.
   •   Evolving digestive systems capable of processing alternative or less nutritious food
       sources.
   •   Developing fat storage mechanisms to endure periods of scarcity.

8. Diversifying or Targeting Alternative Food Sources

Species might shift their focus to alternative resources in their ecosystem. For instance:

   •   Herbivores might target different plants or parts of plants, such as seeds instead of leaves.
   •   Carnivores might switch to hunting smaller, more abundant prey or scavenging carrion.

9. Exploiting Symbiotic Relationships

In some cases, species may form or strengthen symbiotic relationships. For instance, mutualistic
relationships with other organisms can provide access to alternative food sources, such as
pollinators relying on non-preferred plants.

Foraging behavior refers to the set of activities and strategies an organism uses to search for,
locate, and obtain food to meet its nutritional and energy needs. This behavior involves decision-making
processes that balance the benefits of acquiring food with the costs, such as energy expenditure, time, and
risk of predation.

Adaptations

If a species' primary food source were to become scarce or unavailable, several adaptations might occur in
its foraging behavior to cope with the change:

Dietary Flexibility: The species may broaden its diet, incorporating alternative food sources. For example,
herbivores might start eating more types of plants or even switch to eating animals if the primary
vegetation becomes scarce. Carnivores might turn to scavenging or consume smaller prey.

Increased Mobility: If food sources become sparse in one area, the species may increase its foraging
range, traveling farther in search of food. This could lead to shifts in home range size or migration
patterns.

Temporal Shifts: The species might change its foraging times. For instance, it could start foraging during
different times of day (e.g., nocturnal animals becoming more diurnal) or seasonally, in order to align with
the availability of new or remaining food sources.

Enhanced Memory or Learning: Species might develop better spatial memory to recall the locations of
food or learn how to exploit new food sources more efficiently. This could involve enhanced cognitive
abilities to track food availability over time.

behaviors. For example, animals may develop tools or new techniques to extract food from
harder-to-reach places, such as using sticks to dig for insects or cracking open shells.

long-term evolutionary changes.

  “A loss of responsiveness to stimuli that convey little or no new information”.

Imprinting with example:
 “Formation of a long lasting behavioral attachment to a particular individual or object
    at a specific stage in life”.
 Examples:
 Seagulls, sensitive period for a parent to bond with its young lasts one to two days. If
   bonding does not occur, parent will not care for the infant, leading to death of the
   offspring.
 Classic experiment of Konrad Lorenz with geese. Konrad Lorenz made goslings to
    imprint on him. Goslings followed him as though he was their mother.
Reflex action:
Reflex action is a sudden and involuntary response to stimuli. A reflex action requires a
reflex arc which consists of:
      Reflex arc components:
      ▪ A sensory organ (receptor),
      ▪ A sensory nerve (afferent nerve),
       ▪ The spinal cord or brain,
       ▪ An intermediate motor or efferent nerve
      .▪ A motor organ or effector.
Web making process:

 • When a spider begins a web, it releases a silk thread. It anchors the thread to some
    object such as a branch.
 • As the spider moves back and forth, it adds more threads, strengthening the web
    and creating a pattern.
  • Lines that go from the center of the web outward are called “radial lines“. They
     support the web.
 • Threads that go around and around the web are called “orb lines.”
 • The main reason spiders spin webs is to catch the prey. When an insect, such as a
    fly, flies into a spider’s web, it gets stuck on the sticky threads.
 • When a spider catches prey in the sticky strands of its web, it approaches the
    trapped insect and uses its fangs to inject venom. The venom either kills or
    paralyzes the prey.
Fixed Action Patterns (Instincts):
 • It is a sequence of unlearned, innate behaviour that is unchangeable.
 • Once initiated; it is usually carried to completion.
 • It is hardwired, however, not purely genetic, may improve with experience.
 • FAP is triggered by an external sensory stimulus known as “sign stimulus”.
Innate behavior:
 “ is inborn or innate sequence of activities which are predictable, species specific,
 genetically controlled and independent of past experience.”
Behavior that is developmentally fixed is called innate behavior. Innate behavior is
controlled by genetics. These behaviors produce responses that are automatic without
any prior experience. Since this type of behavior follows a fixed pattern (FAP) which is
predictable and found in all members of a species it is also called stereotyped
behavior.
 Examples: Early survival, reproduction, kinesis, taxis. Sneezing, shivering, yawning,
   quickly pulling your hand away from a hot surface, blinking your eyes.
Types of innate behavior:
 There are different types of innate or stereotyped behavior.
    1) Taxis
    2) Irritability
    3) Kinesis
    4) Instincts
    5) Reflexes
    6) Motivation
Learned behavior:
Learned behavior is one that an organism develops as a result of experience.
Thorpe defined learning as a long lasting adaptive change in behavior resulting from
past experience; hence it is acquired during the life time of an individual.
 Examples:
 1. By watching their mother, baby ducks learn how to avoid danger and to know what
    is good to eat. This is an example of learned behavior.
 2. Prairie dogs learns by experience to only make alarm calls when they hear
    predators.

Reflex action: Reflex action is a sudden and involuntary response to stimuli.

Reflex arc components: A sensory organ (receptor), A sensory nerve ( afferent
nerve), The spinal cord or brain, An intermediate motor or efferent nerve, A motor
organ or effector.
Steps of Reflex Action:
1. The stimulus is received by the receptor or sense organ which sets up a sensory
impulse.
2. This impulse is transmitted to the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord)
through the intermediate nerve.
3. This motor impulse is transmitted to the effector or motor organ, muscles and glands
which either contract or secrete in response to the stimulus.

Process of web making:
• When a spider begins a web, it releases a silk thread. It anchors the thread to some
object such as a branch.
• As the spider moves back and forth, it adds more threads, strengthening the web and
creating a pattern.
 • Lines that go from the center of the web outward are called "radial lines“. They
support the web.
• Threads that go around and around the web are called "orb lines."
• The main reason spiders spin webs is to catch the prey. When an insect, such as a fly,
flies into a spider's web, it gets stuck on the sticky threads.
• When a spider catches prey in the sticky strands of its web, it approaches the trapped
insect and uses its fangs to inject venom. The venom either kills or paralyzes the prey.
